messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mei Lin was 76, married, and had spent most of her adult life working as a mechanic, a trade she still kept up part-time because she liked the order of engines and the usefulness of her hands. What brought her to treatment was not one single collapse but the way the world had become hard to move through after a period of stalking by a man she had once encountered through work. The fear began when he started appearing where he had no reason to be, lingering near her garage, watching her leave, and later showing up close to home. At the time she tried to explain it to her husband and to herself, but whenever she began to tell the story she lost the thread and could not finish; the details came to her in sharp, almost photographic pieces, like still images rather than a continuous account. She would see his face in one frame, the parking lot in another, the angle of her own hands on the steering wheel, and then she would feel herself pushing the memory away before she could bring it all into words. That broken way of remembering had made the event hard to place in time, but it also left the fear lodged in her body as if the man could still appear at any moment.

Since then, Mei Lin had become intensely alert and watchful. Even inside her own home she felt on guard, listening for footsteps, glancing at windows and the front door, and when she was outside she frequently looked behind her to check whether someone was following. The more she watched for danger, the more often the old images came back in fragments. Seeing a similar vehicle near the garage, hearing a footstep behind her in a shop aisle, or catching the smell of soil and outdoor earth after rain could pull her back into those photographic scenes before she had time to steady herself. When the images arrived, they did not come as a story she could control; they came as a sudden, vivid flash, and afterward she found herself tense and scanning again, convinced she had to stay prepared because forgetting even for a moment might give danger a chance to get close. The more she remained on guard, the more those fragments crowded in.

What had surprised her most was that even times that should have felt safe did not stay that way. Stress at work, such as a busy day in the garage or a small mistake with a repair, seemed to thin her sense of control and make the memories rise more quickly. So did moments when she felt happy or relaxed. If she sat in the backyard with her husband, or felt briefly content after a good meal, the ease itself could make her mind swing back to the stalking, as if relaxation left her exposed. In those moments the memory would surface again in those same still pictures, and she would pull away from it almost immediately, shortening the thought before it could fully form. Once the memory had been stirred, she became more watchful again, checking the driveway, checking behind her, and scanning the yard even when she knew intellectually she was at home. That vigilance then made ordinary outdoor smells feel charged, especially the smell of soil when she walked past the garden beds near her house or stepped out of the garage, because the smell was now tied to the sharpness of the remembered scenes and seemed to announce that something was about to happen.

Over weeks and months, Mei Lin organized her days around this tension. She still came to the shop, but she moved more carefully, keeping herself near exits and avoiding unnecessary errands after dark. Her husband noticed she no longer relaxed easily in places she had once enjoyed, and at home she had become harder to settle, as though part of her was always listening. She finally sought help when she realized she was spending more time checking behind her than paying attention to the present, and when even a brief feeling of calm could be followed by the sudden return of those vivid, unfinished images. What she hoped for now was simple: to be able to speak about what happened without losing her place, to walk into her own home without feeling on guard, and to trust that a smell of earth or a moment of peace would not immediately bring the fear rushing back.
